description: We are an interdisciplinary team of students interested in science, technology, space exploration and solving real-world problems through innovative ideas. Our backgrounds include Nanotechnology and Biomedical engineering, and we are specially interested in combining science, engineering, and software to create practical solutions.
summary:
We propose a portable biomonitoring system designed to continuously assess astronauts' health through core body temperature (CBT), oxygen saturation (SpO₂), and cardiovascular parameters. Integrated with a mobile application, it establishes individual physiological baselines, tracks trends, and detects deviations, enabling personalized assessments and early anomaly detection. These data will also support future AI-driven predictive health capabilities.

Its dual-mode architecture combines continuous monitoring with autonomous decision support through real-time analysis, personalized thresholds, and automated alerts. This enables timely responses to potential health risks, even when communication with mission control is limited or unavailable, supporting medical decision-making during space missions.

Beyond space exploration, this technology could advance healthcare on Earth through remote monitoring and personalized, predictive care. By developing solutions to protect astronauts in extreme environments, we create opportunities for more accessible and resilient healthcare systems.
details:
BIOMONITOR PORTABLE SYSTEM

1. Overview & The Problem

Long-duration missions beyond Low Earth Orbit expose astronauts to altered gravity, space radiation, isolation, and closed-loop environments that induce cardiovascular deconditioning, space anemia, thermoregulatory shifts, and bone demineralization. Because Earth-to-Mars communication latency reaches up to 20 minutes one-way (40 minutes round-trip) alongside periodic solar conjunction blackouts and the absence of cellular infrastructure, crews cannot rely on real-time ground medical intervention. Astronauts (who are rarely physicians) require an autonomous, wearable decision-support system capable of detecting physiological anomalies locally and delivering immediate, actionable protocols before acute symptoms compromise crew safety.

2. How It Works: The "Collect – Analyze – Guide" Pipeline

Our academic prototype is designed as a wearable finger module with non-contact infrared thermometry (scalable to a hermetic intra-suit vest) operating in dual autonomous mode without external network dependence.

Collect (Biometric Acquisition)

A MAX30102 optical sensor captures Heart Rate (HR) and Peripheral Oxygen Saturation (SpO2 ), while an MLX90614 non-contact infrared sensor measures Core Body Temperature (CBT). To counter motion artifacts and electromagnetic interference, the firmware applies a 5-sample moving average filter and separates wireless antennas from the analog acquisition zone.

Analyze (Edge Threshold Evaluation

A PIC18F4550 microcontroller (with scalable architecture toward ESP32) programmed in Embedded C compares live readings against the astronaut's calibrated resting baseline and mission-stage thresholds, enforcing strict alert priority (Red > Yellow > Green). 

Guide (Immediate Firmware Alerts & App Interface)

Rather than requiring manual interpretation during emergencies, the microcontroller directly triggers physical status LEDs (Green, Yellow, Red) and transmits a structured UART/serial text string via an HC-05 Bluetooth module (configured via AT commands) to a custom MIT App Inventor dashboard. Every alert displays an ultra-short, two-part instruction readable in under three seconds: a Medical Action (self-care, hydration with electrolytes, rest, or exercise) and a Non-Medical Action (inspecting ECLSS CO2 scrubbers, suit pressure seals, or cooling fans). The app also integrates personal baseline setup, a usage guide mode, preventive checkup timers, and an automated 3-minute Stand Test. 

3. Adaptive Mission Logic (Earth – Space – Mars) & Engineering Factors

Because human physiology adapts across gravitational regimes, fixed terrestrial thresholds cause false alarms or missed clinical events. Active intervention during Launch (3g–4g) is intentionally excluded because crews are restrained in 5-point harnesses with pressurized gloves and intense mechanical vibrations introduce severe optical motion artifacts. Furthermore, because no human clinical dataset exists on the Martian surface (0.38g), our system avoids speculative estimations and instead applies conservative, evidence-based thresholds:

4. Tools, Hardware, Software & Scientific Sources

Hardware & Protections: PIC18F4550 microcontroller (scalable to ESP32), MAX30102 pulse oximeter/HR sensor, MLX90614 infrared thermometer, HC-05 Bluetooth module, status LEDs, hermetic enclosure against abrasive Martian dust, internal thermal monitoring, and periodic memory/optical integrity checks against ionizing radiation (SEE, TID, and LED displacement damage). Software & Languages: Embedded C (threshold logic, moving-average filtering, UART serial framing), AT commands (Bluetooth setup), and MIT App Inventor (mobile UI, baseline personalization, preventive timers, and automated Stand Test). NASA & Peer-Reviewed Data: NASA HRP 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight & Evidence Reports, NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2, Nature Reviews Cardiology, Nature Medicine, Circulation, JAMA Network Open, Journal of Applied Physiology, and npj Microgravity.

5. Creativity, Benefits & Intended Impact

The project's core innovation lies in bridging hardware-level LED triage with ultra-short medical and operational (non-medical) commands generated directly by the microcontroller firmware— empowering non-physician astronauts to resolve both physiological distress and life-support anomalies without Earth connectivity. Beyond serving as an accessible, low-cost academic platform for analog spaceflight research and remote terrestrial telemedicine, our next development phase will integrate an onboard physiological database paired with a personalized Artificial Intelligence (AI) model for predictive health analytics and autonomous radiation-induced fault detection.

3. NASA HRP. Evidence Report: Risk of Orthostatic Intolerance During Re-exposure to Gravity. NASA Johnson Space Center.

4. Trudel, G., Shahin, N., Ramsay, T., Laneuville, O., & Louati, H. (2022). Hemolysis contributes to anemia during long-duration space flight. Nature Medicine, 28(1), 59–62.

8. Fu, Q., Shibata, S., Hastings, J. L., et al. (2019). Impact of Prolonged Spaceflight on Orthostatic Tolerance During Ambulation and Blood Pressure Profiles in Astronauts. Circulation, 140(9), 729–738.
